title: The Wazir's Son and the Bathhouse Keeper

keywords: the wazir's son and the hammam-keeper's wife
full_text:
The spoiled son of a grand vizier of Cairo grew up surrounded by luxury, never understanding the value of an honest day’s labor. Believing that common working people existed merely to serve his whims, he mocked the artisans and traders in the bazaar.

One afternoon, seeking shelter from a sudden thunderstorm, the youth stepped into a modest public bathhouse kept by an elderly, cheerful man named Abu Qasim.

Seeing the shivering young nobleman, Abu Qasim did not ask for his purse. He gave him dry linen, poured warm water scented with wild chamomile over his head, and shared his humble supper of roasted chickpeas, flatbread, and fresh goat cheese.

While the storm raged, Abu Qasim spoke with warm humor of the daily joys of honest toil, of serving travelers, and of the peaceful sleep that comes to those who earn their bread with clean hands.

The vizier’s son was struck by the radiant contentment in the old keeper’s eyes—a peace that none of the wealthy courtiers in his father’s palace possessed.

The youth returned to his palace, embraced his father, and said: 'Father, for twenty years you gave me gold, but today a bathhouse keeper gave me wisdom.'

The young nobleman renounced his idle arrogance, apprenticed himself to an architectural master, and built public baths and hospitals for the poor of Cairo, retaining Abu Qasim as his lifelong counselor.
moral: Humility and true friendship are found in simple labor, not in the arrogant luxury of palaces.
